narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about you. The single most important factor was that you plan to attend law school part-time. Among students who were admitted, only 7% planned to study part-time; the vast majority attended full-time. This choice strongly pushed the prediction toward failure.

Your first-year grades were the second most influential factor. You placed in the fourth decile of your class, noticeably below the average of sixth decile among accepted students. This weaker early performance also increased the model’s estimate of your risk of failing the bar.

Your third-year grades worked in the opposite direction. Placing in the seventh decile, slightly above the average for accepted students, gave the model some reassurance that your performance had improved and helped pull the prediction back toward passing. However, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the combined effect of part-time study plans and early academic standing.

The model therefore concluded you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam, leading to the rejection. To improve your chances in future applications, consider attending full-time if possible and strengthening your first-year performance through targeted academic support. These two changes would likely have the largest impact on how a similar model evaluates your profile. (248 words)
